newsitem.title: GERMANY: Air Zimbabwe sees rising cargo volumes in Germany.
newsitem.headline: Air Zimbabwe sees rising cargo volumes in Germany.

text.p: Air Zimbabwe said it expected its air cargo volumes in Germany to rise to 400 tonnes this year after it took control of its own sales activities.
The airline's cargo sales executive for Germany, Carlos Sanchez, told Reuters this would be a 40 percent share of the estimated total Germany to Zimbabwe air cargo market of 1,000 tonnes.
He added that sales had picked up in recent months although revenue had been hit by a 25 percent rates fall in the last 12 months.
The rates fall meant the airline would not be able to achieve its financial targets in Germany this year, he told Reuters in an interview.
But he added: "We are keeping our prices stable. We have a good price for the service which we can provide with a direct flight."
The African airline flies Tuesdays and Saturdays from Frankfurt to Harare with a Boeing 767-200 with a maximum freight capacity of 13 tonnes.
Air Zimbabwe ended the contract of the former gsa, Aerotrans, last spring since it represented at the same time several airlines flying to southern Africa, Sanchez said.
"When the airline presents itself to customers it is very different than when it is a gsa. Sales are now going much better" he added.
The airline had recorded cargo load factors of 81 percent and 88 percent in January and February, he pointed out.
Sanchez claimed he had also won back clients who switched to rival carrier Affretair during a one-week Air Zimbabwe pilots' strike in March.
"Our ace is our Saturday flight allowing forwarders to deliver on Friday evening," he said.
The twice-weekly Affretair freighter flights from Amsterdam departed earlier in the week while Lufthansa only served Harare on the return leg from Johannesburg, he pointed out.
Sanchez said goods flown as air cargo from Germany to Zimbabwe included agricultural machinery and fertilisers and chemical products of companies such as Bayer AG, Hoechst AG and BASF AG.
About 75 percent of the airline's freight ex-Germany was destined for Harare or Bulawayo, with very little transshipment cargo for South Africa, he added.
"Zimbabwe is a stable market. What could grow is the transport of computers and telecommunications equipment," he said.
Northbound cargo for Europe was virtually exclusively fruit and vegetables on a year-round basis depending on the type of perishable product, he added.
